source.title: Would this change your answer? Evaluating Explanations of LLM Behavior In The Wild with Counterfactual Experiments
source.authors: Adam Karvonen; Euan Ong; Subhash Kantamneni; Samuel Marks

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper evaluates activation-based tools for predicting prompt-counterfactual behavior, but does not test neuron poles, neuron-level explanations, or neurons as units of analysis.
record.gate_note: The reported tool results concern whether activation-oracle, NLA, and SAE outputs improve a predictor's counterfactual behavior forecasts over a transcript-only baseline. They do not measure the interpretability of individual neurons or explanations of neuron activations as named jobs, so they are recorded as related findings with versions ["none"], not as tests of V1–V7.
record.test_reason: The paper asks whether three activation-reading tools (activation oracles, natural-language autoencoders, and SAE features with auto-interp labels) help an external agent predict prompt-counterfactual behaviour. It never examines individual neurons or neuron poles. It does not score neuron or feature explanations by simulating activations. It builds no attribution graphs and tests no vision neurons. Its 'counterfactual simulatability' concerns explanations of model behaviour, not explanations of where a unit fires. So no result bears on V1–V7. The originals are not cited; 'discusses' is the closest available label, and the study neither tests nor uses the claim.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct, but incomplete. The authors also present CHIVE as a scalable way to generate counterfactual-grounded explanations. They report that training models to predict their own counterfactual behaviour generalizes to held-out and hint settings, with no evidence of privileged access. Training on open-ended explanations gives mixed results.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates activation-reading tools by whether an external predictor can forecast prompt-counterfactual behavior; it does not audit individual neuron poles or test neuron explanations against unseen activations.
record.method_sensitivity: On Gemma-3-27B-IT, changing tool-call budgets (2, 5, 10) and NLA/SAE token positions per call (16, 32, 64) did not yield uplift; all reported 95% bootstrap intervals straddled zero. Predictor family changes the magnitude of tool effects, including downlift for Gemini-3.1-Pro with NLA and SAE.

fits_no_version.finding: AO, NLA and SAE outputs give no uplift over a transcript-only predictor of prompt-counterfactual behaviour on Gemma-3-27B-IT and Qwen3-8B. Gemini-3.1-Pro is hurt by the NLA and SAE. NLA outputs state the X-causes-Y relation in only 0.6% of positive claims.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Current activation-reading tools do not improve prediction of counterfactual behaviour for naturally occurring LLM behaviours.

record.problems: The evaluation is a proxy based on prompt counterfactuals, and the authors note possible distribution shifts from cases where interpretability tools are most needed. Several exploratory analyses use LLM judges. Table 4 gives no numerical confidence-interval endpoints; exact scores for some main results are shown only in figures or described in text.
record.rows_left_out: No rows left out. Tool-prediction results are included as related findings, not as measurements of neuron-level interpretability.

untested.parts: Qwen3-32B neuron-pole audit shares (about 90/7/2–4%); Qwen3-32B appears only as a released dataset target.
Neuron interpretability shares across dense and MoE models and across scale.
InceptionV1 polysemantic examples, pose, and recursive generalization.
Effect of architecture, regularization and tools on the share of interpretable neurons.
Neuron-based attribution graphs compared with replacement models.
Whether explanations from activating examples predict where a neuron fires.
Simulation-based scoring of neuron explanations and the share of neurons scoring well.

record.verdict_notes: Several Table 4 rows have swapped conditions or values, include a duplicate (r14), or invent cells (r17, r18). The Table 4 grid is: tool-call sweep at 32 positions; position sweep at 5 calls; AO has no position sweep. SAE auto-interp labels are used as tool inputs but are never evaluated as explanations of activations, so nothing here bears on V6 or V7.

versions.untested_parts: The Qwen3-32B pole audit and its percentages are not measured.
No neuron-pole interpretability shares are measured across models or scale.
No InceptionV1 cat-and-car example or pose/generalization account is tested.
The study does not compare architecture, regularization, tools, or interpretable-neuron shares.
No attribution graphs or neuron-based circuit reconstructions are evaluated.
The study does not test neuron explanations against their activating examples or predict neuron firing.
It does not score neuron explanations by simulating activations on new text or report the share of neurons with good scores.

relation.reason: Fits as the loosest available relation. The paper does not test the claim and never mentions neurons.

tranche.reason: The paper evaluates activation-reading tools (AO, NLA, SAE features with auto-interp labels) for predicting counterfactual behaviour. It never examines neurons and does not test or use any claim version.

source_check.notes: Table 4 holds two sweeps: call budget (2/5/10) at 32 positions, and positions (16/32/64) at a 5-call budget. In the record, r02 and r03 take 16-position, 5-call cells, r06 and r16 have wrong values, and r08 and r09 have the wrong position count. No row bears on any version. The Gemini downlift is called significant, but no statistic is given.

statements.correction: Text: no tool improves on the transcript-only baseline for Gemma-3-27B-IT or Qwen3-8B. With Gemini-3.1-Pro as the predictor on Gemma claims, AUROC is 0.654 with NLA and 0.746 with SAE, against a 0.793 baseline; the authors call this a significant downlift. An explicit X-causes-Y statement appears in 0.6% of positive claims (3 of 479; Opus 4.8 judge).
